## Learning objectives {#ch11-01 .balanced .stepwise}

- Classify rows and compare calendar periods.
- Use windows without losing row detail.
- Organize and check a chain of CTEs.
- Save a monthly measure as a view in the working copy.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: introduce the tools needed for a reusable monthly explanation. Allow 60 seconds. The annual comparison located the change in recorded hours but did not show its timing. Students will keep the same accounting question while changing the grain and comparison window. Ask what a manager needs to distinguish an old level shift from a current deterioration. Transition: state the monitoring questions.
:::

# Classify the hours and costs {#ch11-module-2}

::: {.notes}
Turn transaction categories into measures whose accounting treatment is explicit.
:::

## The controller needs the timing of the change {#ch11-03 .balanced .stepwise}

When did indirect time appear?

Is the relationship still changing?

How much is overtime, and where is it recorded?

::: {.notes}
Purpose: motivate monthly measures and partitions. Allow 60 seconds. An annual total can combine very different months and work centers. A monthly ratio can be volatile because output is uneven, so the measure will also use a trailing window. Keep the questions distinct: level, trend, overtime share, and location. Ask which one a single total cannot answer. Transition: classify payroll lines.
:::

## CASE assigns the first matching category {#ch11-04 .balanced .sql-example}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_query-payroll_categories.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: read the classification excerpt from the public payroll query. Allow 90 seconds. Conditions are tested in order, and the first true branch supplies the value. ELSE handles all remaining line types. That catch-all needs validation against the observed categories; a new type could otherwise be silently misclassified. This excerpt is the SELECT portion of the full grouped query. Ask students which type would fall through to ELSE. Transition: compare the classified amounts.
:::

## Employee deductions are not an added employer cost {#ch11-05 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_categories.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect classification with accounting meaning. Allow 60-90 seconds. The categories sum different payroll line types. Employee deductions are withheld from employee pay, so adding them again to earnings would overstate employer cost. Hourly pay, salaries, and employer taxes and benefits are the relevant components for this control. Ask students to state the reconciliation before calculating it. Transition: compare with the ledger.
:::

## The cost categories tie to account 1090 {#ch11-06 .balanced .stepwise}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_payroll.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: verify that the classification preserves the intended cost. Allow 60 seconds. The component sum excludes employee deductions and agrees with the payroll source debits in manufacturing clearing. Agreement supports the classification under the current line-type population. It does not test employment validity, approval, or whether the hours occurred. Ask which new payroll category would require updating the classification. Transition: examine CASE and missing values.
:::

## A missing value needs an explicit CASE condition {#ch11-07 .balanced .sql-example .stepwise}

```sql
CASE
  WHEN CompletedDate IS NULL THEN 'Open'
  ELSE 'Completed'
END
```

A simple `CASE column WHEN NULL` cannot match NULL.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish the searched and simple CASE forms. Allow 60 seconds. This illustrative expression tests missingness directly. The simple form compares one expression with candidate values using equality, which does not match NULL. The order and ELSE branch should cover the intended population without overlap. Ask how a third business status would change the rule. Transition: give periods a consistent representation.
:::

## Dates become period keys {#ch11-08 .balanced .sql-example .stepwise}

```sql
strftime('%Y-%m', WorkDate)
date(WorkDate, 'start of month')
julianday(CompletedDate) - julianday(ReleasedDate)
```

Use text periods consistently, and state the elapsed-time unit.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: introduce the date expressions used by the public tutorials. Allow 60-90 seconds. strftime creates a year-month label and date applies modifiers in sequence. julianday permits subtraction in days. SQLite's date functions depend on supported representations; malformed source text can yield NULL. strftime returns text, so compare its year result with a text year or cast it. Ask why grouping only by month number would combine different years. Transition: find the coverage end.
:::

## Profile the gap to month-end {#ch11-09 .balanced .sql-example}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_query-end_of_records.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make the final-month limitation measurable. Allow 90 seconds. The query finds the last work date and derives that month's end using ordered modifiers. The subtraction reports calendar days without time records at the end of the month. It does not prove those days had no work. Ask how including later production completions would distort an hours ratio. Transition: pivot categories into columns.
:::

## Conditional aggregation retains one row per month {#ch11-10 .balanced .sql-example}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_query-hours_by_month.qmd >}}

Excerpt: the direct-hours column of the monthly query.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: show SQL's counterpart to a conditional spreadsheet sum. Allow 60-90 seconds. CASE returns each row's hours only for the chosen labor type, and SUM adds those values within the grouped month. ELSE zero makes the contribution of other labor types explicit. The complete query adds indirect and overtime columns. Ask which GROUP BY is required to get one result per month. Transition: read the early monthly pattern.
:::

## The early months have little indirect time {#ch11-11 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_early-months.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: turn a narrative claim into a visible monthly result. Allow 90 seconds. January is the start-up month. From February through May, indirect hours are very low while direct hours remain substantial; June shows a shift. The zero in March is a recorded result, not proof that the time population is complete. A later audit procedure examines that completeness. Ask what evidence would distinguish a true operating pattern from missing records. Transition: keep ratio denominators visible.
:::

## A conditional ratio needs a matching denominator {#ch11-12 .balanced .stepwise}

Direct overtime / all direct hours.

Indirect overtime / all indirect hours.

A zero denominator produces no meaningful share.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: prevent mixing population definitions in a percentage. Allow 60 seconds. Both numerator and denominator must use the same labor classification and period. A month with no indirect hours has no defined indirect overtime share; do not replace that with a meaningful-looking zero without explanation. The public tutorial compares the two trends separately. Ask why total overtime divided by direct hours would answer a different question. Transition: complete the first tutorial.
:::

Reconcile payroll categories to the ledger.

Check monthly coverage and the last WorkDate.

Interpret overtime shares and work-order lead time.

[Open Tutorial 11.1](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/11-analytical-queries/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-11.1-classifying-the-payroll-and-measuring-the-hours-by-month)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: consolidate CASE, dates, and conditional aggregation. Allow three minutes. Students should inspect the missing or zero denominator cases, identify the partial final month, and document that average work-order lead time more than doubles across the public tutorial's years. Ask each pair for a finding and a qualification. The next module compares rows while keeping them visible. Transition: introduce window functions.

# Compare rows with windows {#ch11-module-14}

::: {.notes}
A window calculation adds a comparison to each result row instead of collapsing the result.
:::

## GROUP BY collapses; OVER preserves rows {#ch11-15 .balanced .stepwise}

**GROUP BY:** one output row per group.

**Window function:** an added value on each result row.

**PARTITION BY:** the rows compared for that value.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: establish the central distinction. Allow 60-90 seconds. A monthly aggregate can first create one row per period; a window then compares those monthly rows. Partitioning by year keeps year-to-date calculations separate without replacing the twelve monthly rows by one annual row. Ask how many rows should remain after adding a running total to twelve months. Transition: define the order within a partition.
:::

## A year-to-date window restarts by year {#ch11-16 .balanced .sql-example}

```sql
SUM(SUM(Debit) - SUM(Credit)) OVER (
  PARTITION BY FiscalYear
  ORDER BY FiscalPeriod
  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
) AS YearToDateGap
```

Teaching expression applied to monthly grouped results.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: explain nested aggregate and window roles. Allow 90 seconds. The inner sums produce the monthly net amount; the outer SUM accumulates those monthly results within each year. The frame explicitly starts at the first row and ends at the current row. The complete query also needs the chapter's account and source-type filters. Ask what happens if the partition is omitted. Transition: distinguish ordering from frame membership.
:::

## A frame counts rows, not calendar months {#ch11-17 .balanced .sql-example .stepwise}

```sql
ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
```

Twelve rows represent twelve months only after coverage is checked.

Missing months need an explicit calendar policy.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: expose the assumption behind a trailing-year label. Allow 60-90 seconds. ROWS selects positions in the ordered result, so a missing month could stretch a twelve-row window over more than a year. The public measure validates one row for every month. When calendar gaps are possible, prepare and validate a calendar sequence instead of relying on the row count alone. Ask whether eleven preceding rows imply a full window near the start of the data. Transition: handle ties in ordering.
:::

## Default frames can include tied rows {#ch11-18 .balanced .stepwise}

An aggregate window with ORDER BY has a default frame.

Rows tied on the ordering value can enter together.

Use an explicit ROWS frame and stable ordering when row steps matter.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: prevent a surprising running total. Allow 60-90 seconds. SQLite's default aggregate frame with ORDER BY includes peers of the current ordering value. A transaction-level running balance can therefore advance in groups when several entries share a date. A ROWS frame defines positions, and a stable extra key defines a reproducible sequence among ties. Ask whether the desired meaning is end-of-day balance or balance after each posting. Transition: compare ranking rules.
:::

## Ranking functions treat ties differently {#ch11-19 .balanced}

| Illustrative score | ROW_NUMBER | RANK | DENSE_RANK |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 100 | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| 90 | 3 | 3 | 2 |

::: {.notes}
Purpose: compare three ranking definitions using an illustration, not Charles River results. Allow 60-90 seconds. ROW_NUMBER assigns consecutive positions, with an additional key needed to decide the order of tied scores. RANK shares a position and leaves a gap; DENSE_RANK shares a position without the gap. Adding a tie-breaker inside the ranking order can remove the tie itself. Ask which definition fits a top-three-distinct-values request. Transition: access an earlier row.
:::

## LAG compares with a prior observation {#ch11-20 .balanced .stepwise}

**PARTITION BY month number:** compare the same month across years.

**ORDER BY year:** define the previous observation.

No earlier observation normally returns NULL.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: read a year-over-year comparison as an ordered lookup. Allow 60-90 seconds. Tutorial 11.2 partitions by fiscal period and orders by year, so LAG supplies the prior available year for that month. A missing year would make prior observation different from immediately previous calendar year. Verify continuity or join through an explicit year offset. The first year's NULL is expected. Transition: filter the calculated rank at an outer level.
:::

## Filter window results in an outer query {#ch11-21 .balanced .sql-example}

```sql
WITH Ranked AS (
  SELECT ...,
    RANK() OVER (...) AS GapRank
  FROM ...
)
SELECT * FROM Ranked
WHERE GapRank <= 3;
```

Pattern only: replace the ellipses with the tutorial query.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: explain why a window alias cannot be filtered in the same WHERE clause. Allow 60-90 seconds. Window functions are calculated after WHERE and grouping at that query level. A CTE or derived table makes the result available to an outer filter. This slide is a structural pattern and intentionally is not executable as written. Ask students where the year grouping and ranking belong. Transition: interpret the top months in context.
:::

## The largest gap months have three pay dates {#ch11-22 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_ranked-gap.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: qualify a monthly ranking with the payroll calendar. Allow 60 seconds. The table shows the highest-ranked month of each year from the public pay-date comparison. These monthly accounting gaps reflect payroll recorded on pay dates, so more pay dates can increase the amount without establishing an operating shock in that month. Ask what work-date measure would help distinguish timing from production activity. Transition: consider work-center comparisons.
:::

## Work-center rankings need a plant control {#ch11-23 .balanced .stepwise}

Compare recorded hours with planned operation hours.

Retain the plant-wide excess beside each center.

A high center ratio needs source-record investigation.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: prevent a local ranking from becoming an unsupported causal claim. Allow 60-90 seconds. Tutorial 11.2 finds high recorded-to-planned ratios at Packing and Quality Assurance even while total plant direct hours remain below plan. The windowed plant total makes that contrast visible without losing each center. The operations and time-record dates need follow-up. Ask what would happen if hours were charged to the wrong operation. Transition: complete the window tutorial.
:::

## Tutorial 11.2: read the comparison before explaining it {#ch11-24 .balanced .stepwise}

Confirm the January reset and first-year NULLs.

Explain rank ties and the pay-date calendar.

Compare work-center and plant-level evidence.

[Open Tutorial 11.2](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/11-analytical-queries/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-11.2-tracking-the-gap-month-by-month)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: check the semantics of each window result. Allow three minutes. Students should locate the outer rank filter and identify which field partitions each calculation. Ask each pair to state why a large monthly gap is not sufficient evidence of lower production efficiency. The next module combines the validated measures into a reusable chain. Transition: name the CTE stages.
:::

# Build and save the monthly measure {#ch11-module-25}

::: {.notes}
Each stage should have a stated grain, a control, and a clear input to the next stage.
:::

## CTEs name the analytical stages {#ch11-26 .balanced .stepwise}

MonthlyOutput: standard hours from completions.

MonthlyHours: direct, indirect, and overtime hours.

Monthly: join the summaries by month.

Trailing: compare aligned windows.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make the long public query teachable in separate steps. Allow 90 seconds. WITH gives each stage a name visible to the statement. Each stage can be selected on its own for inspection before adding the next. The output and hours summaries each need one row per month, and the join should preserve the expected month sequence. Ask what two checks would detect a dropped or duplicated month. Transition: define the output window.
:::

## Align the source coverage before joining {#ch11-27 .balanced .stepwise}

Limit completions to the last recorded WorkDate.

Group output and hours independently by year-month.

Check every month before computing a rolling ratio.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: bring the coverage control into the CTE chain. Allow 60-90 seconds. Limiting completions avoids dividing partial time records by a full final month's output. The pinned public results have 36 consecutive months at the intermediate stages. An inner join would silently drop a month absent from either side, so validate both keys and counts. Ask how the measure should handle an entirely missing month in a future dataset. Transition: aggregate numerators and denominators together.
:::

## A trailing ratio uses the summed evidence {#ch11-28 .balanced .stepwise}

Sum labor hours over the window.

Sum standard hours over the same window.

Divide those totals; do not average monthly ratios.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: preserve activity weighting. Allow 60 seconds. A month with little output should not receive the same weight as a month with much more output merely because both have one row. The public measure uses ratios of window sums for direct, indirect, and total hours. All denominators must be positive and consistently scoped. Ask students to construct a small two-month example in which an average of ratios differs from a ratio of sums. Transition: exclude partial startup windows.
:::

## Require a full twelve-month window {#ch11-29 .balanced .sql-example .stepwise}

```sql
COUNT(*) OVER w AS MonthsInWindow
```

Then retain `MonthsInWindow = 12` in the next query level.

The first complete window ends in December 2024.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish a calculated value from a comparable trailing-year value. Allow 60-90 seconds. The early rows have fewer than twelve observations even though the ROWS frame is syntactically valid. Counting the window exposes that limitation. With 36 consecutive monthly rows, the full-window result contains 25 months. A complete row count still depends on the earlier month-continuity check. Ask why the outer filter must come after the windows are calculated. Transition: read the smoothed result.
:::

## The components show different trends {#ch11-30 .balanced}

![](/_shared/generated/chapter-11/trailing.svg){fig-alt="Trailing twelve-month direct, indirect, and total labor hours per standard hour, with direct solid, indirect dotted, and total dashed lines." width=95%}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: interpret the ratio of window sums. Allow 90 seconds. The direct, indirect, and total series use the same aligned standard-hour denominator. Indirect hours rise and then level off, while direct hours continue increasing through the later period. The total combines both. The last point includes the source-coverage qualification. Ask why smoothing helps see the pattern but cannot validate the underlying time records. Transition: save the measure without duplicating its results.
:::

## A view saves the query definition {#ch11-31 .balanced .stepwise}

Create **MonthlyLaborEfficiency** in the working copy.

A view stores a query, rather than a frozen result.

Save the SQL script and use **Write Changes** for the view.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish a reusable database object from an exported table. Allow 60-90 seconds. Creating the view changes the working database, unlike the earlier SELECT statements. Confirm the copy's path before running the public DROP and CREATE statements. The script remains the reproducible definition, while Write Changes persists the object in DB Browser. A view does not guarantee row order. Ask how a changed source row would affect the next query of the view. Transition: query the saved object.
:::

## The saved view has a short consumer query {#ch11-32 .balanced .sql-example}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_query-query_view.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: show the instructor or manager's reusable interface. Allow 60 seconds. The view supplies the long analytical chain, while the consumer chooses the displayed period and ordering. Tutorial 11.3 compares the twelve fiscal 2026 rows with the full query. A successful CREATE command by itself would not prove equivalence. Ask students to locate one month in both results. Transition: read a focused excerpt from that result.
:::

## The final months retain the component detail {#ch11-33 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-11/_view.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect the chart with native editable numerical evidence. Allow 60 seconds. These are the final three rows of the public fiscal 2026 view, showing the trailing direct, indirect, and total ratios. Rounding may make a displayed component sum differ slightly from the displayed total. The full view also retains the unsmoothed monthly ratio and trailing overtime share. Validate the 36-month intermediate sequence.
